title: defer: LIFO order and when arguments are evaluated
summary: defer schedules a call for when the function returns, in reverse order, with its arguments evaluated immediately. Deferred closures can rewrite named results; os.Exit skips them all.

examples.title: Last in, first out, and arguments evaluated at defer time

annotations.note: Deferred calls run when main returns, not at the end of each loop iteration, and in reverse order. A loop that opens a file per iteration and defers Close keeps every file open until return.
The arguments of a deferred call are evaluated when the defer statement runs, so this line prints 1 although x is 2 by then.
A closure reads x when it finally runs, so it prints 2. Pick the form that captures the value you mean.

examples.title: Deferred closures can change named results, and recover from panics

annotations.note: The return statement assigns port and err first; then the deferred closure runs and can replace err. One place adds context to every error path.
All three returns pass through the deferred wrapper, including the range check added later. Nobody can forget the context.
recover stops a panic only when called directly by a deferred function. Here the integer division by zero becomes an ordinary error value.
This cleanup never prints: the expected output has a single line.
os.Exit ends the process immediately, without running deferred calls. log.Fatal and log.Fatalf call os.Exit(1), so in a server they skip the cleanup you deferred.

use_cases: Releasing resources right after acquiring them: defer f.Close(), defer mu.Unlock(), defer rows.Close()
Adding context to every error of a function in one deferred closure
Turning a panic into an error at a boundary (an HTTP handler, a worker goroutine)
strengths: Cleanup sits next to the acquisition, so it can't drift away from it, unlike a finally block at the bottom of a long Java method
Runs on every return path and during panics, which try/finally also does, but without the extra nesting
Argument evaluation at defer time makes defer logDuration(time.Now()) work with no closure
weaknesses: Defers are per function, not per block: in loops they pile up until the function returns
os.Exit and log.Fatal bypass them, so cleanup depends on how the program ends
An error returned by a deferred Close is easy to ignore; handling it needs a named result and a closure

pitfalls.title: defer in a loop
pitfalls.detail: Each iteration's defer waits for the function to return. Move the loop body into its own function so each defer runs per iteration.
pitfalls.bad: for _, p := range paths { f, _ := os.Open(p); defer f.Close() }
pitfalls.good: for _, p := range paths { if err := process(p); err != nil { return err } } // process defers Close

pitfalls.title: log.Fatal in a function with defers
pitfalls.detail: It calls os.Exit(1); deferred cleanup never runs. Return the error and exit from main after cleanup instead.

pitfalls.title: Expecting a deferred call to see later changes
pitfalls.detail: defer fmt.Println(x) captures x now. Use a closure if you want the value at return time.

quiz.q: x := 1; defer fmt.Println(x); x = 2. What prints when the function returns?
quiz.why: Arguments are evaluated when the defer statement executes.

quiz.q: Three defers A, B, C are registered in that order. In which order do they run?
quiz.why: Deferred calls run last in, first out.

quiz.q: Where does recover() stop a panic?
options: Only when called directly by a deferred function
quiz.why: Called anywhere else, recover returns nil and the panic continues.

further_reading.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: Defer statements

body:
## Concept

`defer f(args)` schedules `f` to run when the surrounding function returns, whether it
returns normally or panics. Deferred calls run in last-in, first-out order. The function
value and its arguments are evaluated when the `defer` statement executes; only the call
is delayed. Because deferred functions run after the return values are set, a deferred
closure can read and change named results, and it is the only place where `recover`
stops a panic.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java/JS: `defer` replaces most `try/finally` blocks, and it sits next to the
  acquisition instead of at the end of the method.
- Python: similar to a `with` block's exit, but tied to the function, not to a block.
- C++: like a destructor-based scope guard (RAII), but explicit and scoped to the whole
  function.
- `os.Exit` skipping defers matches Java's `System.exit` skipping `finally` and Node's
  `process.exit`. Python's `sys.exit` differs: it raises `SystemExit`, so `finally` and
  `with` blocks still run.

## Design notes

Write the `defer` on the line right after a successful acquisition (`f, err :=
os.Open(p); if err != nil { return err }; defer f.Close()`). If a loop acquires
resources, put the loop body in its own function. Use `recover` only at boundaries you
own, such as an HTTP handler or a worker goroutine, and convert the panic to an error
there; recovering everywhere hides bugs. In `main`, prefer returning errors to a single
exit point over calling `log.Fatal` deep in the code, so deferred cleanup still runs.

expected.lifo-args:
end of main body
closure reads x when it runs: 2
argument evaluated at defer time: 1
deferred in loop: 2
deferred in loop: 1
deferred in loop: 0
expected.named-result:
8080 <nil>
0 parse port "http": strconv.Atoi: parsing "http": invalid syntax
0 parse port "70000": out of range
3 <nil>
0 recovered: runtime error: integer divide by zero
